steps.text: Check response: Shake shoulders and shout 'Are you okay?'
If no response, tilt head back and lift chin to open airway.
Check breathing: Look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for 10 seconds.
If NOT breathing normally, call emergency services immediately and fetch an AED if available.
Start CPR: Place the heel of one hand in the center of the chest, other hand on top. Push hard and fast (100-120 compressions/min, 2-2.4 inches deep). Allow full chest recoil.
If trained, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. If untrained, stick to Hands-Only CPR.
Turn on AED and follow voice prompts. Do not touch the person while the AED is analyzing or shocking.
Ensure your own safety. Put on gloves if available.
Find the source of the bleeding. Expose the wound if necessary.
Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound using a clean cloth, sterile dressing, or hands.
Maintain pressure constantly. Do NOT remove the cloth if it soaks through; add more layers on top.
If bleeding is from an arm or leg, elevate the injured limb above the level of the heart if possible.
If life-threatening bleeding doesn't stop, apply a tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound (not on a joint). Note the time it was applied.
Keep the victim warm to prevent shock and wait for emergency services.
Ensure the person is breathing normally.

Place them in the Recovery Position: kneel beside them, straighten their legs, place the arm nearest to you at a right angle, bring the far arm across their chest, and pull the far knee up. Roll them towards you onto their side.
Tilt their head back slightly to keep the airway open.
Call emergency services immediately.
Monitor breathing constantly until help arrives. Do NOT give them anything to eat or drink.
Do NOT move the injured person unless they are in immediate danger. Moving them can worsen the injury.
Control any bleeding by applying pressure to the edges of the wound, avoiding the exposed bone.
Immobilize the injured area. Use a splint (rolled up newspaper, umbrella, piece of wood) padded with clothing if trained, otherwise keep it supported in the position found.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth to the injured area to reduce swelling and pain.
Call for medical help or arrange transport to a hospital.
Treat for shock: keep them calm, warm, and lying down (if the injury allows).
Stop the burning process: remove the person from the source, extinguish flames (Stop, Drop, and Roll).
Cool the burn immediately with cool (not freezing cold) running water for at least 20 minutes.
Remove constricting items like jewelry, belts, or tight clothing near the burn before swelling begins. Do NOT remove clothing stuck to the burn.
Cover the burn loosely with sterile, non-fluffy dressing, or cling film (Saran wrap).
Do NOT apply ice, butter, ointments, or pop blisters. Seek medical help for severe or large burns.
Ask 'Are you choking?' If they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot cough, breathe, or speak, support their chest and lean them forward.
Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.
If unsuccessful, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver): stand behind, wrap arms around waist, make a fist above the navel, grab fist with the other hand, pull inward and upward.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is dislodged. If they become unconscious, start CPR.
Recognize signs: pale/cold/clammy skin, rapid/weak pulse, fast/shallow breathing, confusion.
Lay the person down flat on their back. Elevate their legs about 12 inches unless it causes pain or a spinal injury is suspected.
Call emergency services immediately. Shock is life-threatening.
Keep the person warm with a blanket or coat. Do NOT give them food or drink.
Reassure them, loosen tight clothing, and monitor breathing. Be ready to start CPR if breathing stops.
Face: Ask them to smile. Does one side of the face droop?
Arms: Ask them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward?
Speech: Ask them to repeat a simple phrase. Is their speech slurred or strange?
Time: If you observe any of these signs, call emergency services immediately and note the time the symptoms started.
Keep them calm and resting. Do NOT give them food, drink, or medication (not even aspirin).
Recognize signs: severe chest pain/pressure spreading to arms, neck, jaw, or back; shortness of breath; sweating.
Call emergency services immediately.
Have the person sit down, rest, and keep calm. Loosen tight clothing.
If they are prescribed angina medication (like nitroglycerin), help them take it.
If they are fully conscious and not allergic, offer them a regular adult aspirin (300mg) to chew slowly.
Monitor constantly. Be prepared to start CPR if they lose consciousness and stop breathing.
Do NOT try to restrain the person or stop their movements.
Protect them from injury: clear the area of hard or sharp objects, place something soft (like a jacket) under their head.
Do NOT put anything in their mouth.
Time the seizure. If it lasts longer than 5 minutes, call an ambulance.
Once the seizure stops, roll them into the recovery position, check breathing, and reassure them as they recover.
Suspect a spinal injury if there's a serious fall, vehicle accident, or head trauma.
Call emergency services immediately.
Do NOT move the person unless there is immediate life-threatening danger (e.g., fire).
Keep the person's head, neck, and spine perfectly aligned. Hold their head still with your hands on both sides of their ears to prevent movement.
If you must open the airway, use the jaw-thrust maneuver instead of tilting the head back.
